item.title: The Daily Star – Before Plassey: The origins of the East India Company’s land grab in Bengal
item.description:
In late 1698, Charles Eyre, soon to be appointed governor of Fort William in Bengal, persuaded the viceroy, Prince Azim ush Shan, to grant the East India Company a nishan conferring zamindari rights over the three small townships of Sutanuti, Kalkata and Govindpur in exchange for Rs 16,000 and a liberal disbursement of bribes. It was a move later described by Walter Firminger as the most significant and enduring step taken by the Company between 1690 and 1757 (Walter Firminger, Historical Introduction to the Bengal Portion of ‘The Fifth Report’, Cambray, Calcutta, 1917, p. 374). Firminger has to be taken seriously, and so I wish to investigate briefly how the events of 1698 can be situated within the Company’s quest to acquire territory, in the course of which it transformed from a venture concerned principally, but not exclusively, with commerce and trade into a colonising power that came to rule over large parts of the Indian subcontinent (see my Land, Law and Empire: The Origins of British Territorial Power in India, Cambridge University Press, 2025, on which I have drawn here).

The acquisition of land in India has attracted scholarly interest, but for understandable reasons, the events of the eighteenth century have tended to provide the focus. This was a period, after all, when, following Clive’s victory at Palashi in 1757, the Company acquired territory in Bengal and Bihar on a scale that dwarfed its earlier territorial gains. Compared with the enormity of this land grab, the acquisitions of the seventeenth century were minute, and yet I suspected that in the early decades of the Company, the legal, economic and political foundations were laid for the wholesale plunder that was to follow (see Philip Stern, The Company State: Corporate Sovereignty and the Early Modern Foundation of the British Empire in India, Oxford University Press, 2011; and David Veevers, The Origins of the British Empire in Asia, 1600–1750, Cambridge University Press, 2019). 
 
A modern reconstruction shows Sutanuti, Kalikata and Govindpur, the three settlements over which the East India Company acquired zamindari rights in 1698. Map: P. K. Niyogi/Wikimedia Commons.

Indeed, the signs were there from the very start. Hidden amidst the technicalities of the Company's 1600 charter was a clause that empowered it to acquire, retain and dispose of land, not a provision, it has to be said, that we would expect to find in the founding charter of a private, joint-stock company putatively engaged in commerce. The limited power of these seemingly hubristic sentiments, however, was soon exposed by the conditions early factors encountered in India. Not only were they treated with disdain by Mughal authorities, but the futility of the notion that land could be annexed in the face of opposition from an empire with a massive land army soon came to be recognised. Somewhat against the odds, however, the Company was able to lease a commodious house at the great port of Surat, but the factors were only too aware of their vulnerabilities. They could not resist threats to vacate the premises at a moment’s notice, and Mughal officials repeatedly denied them permission to convert the factory into a defensible space by fortifying it.

Frustrated by the intransigence of Mughal authorities and repeated failures to consolidate its position at Surat, the Company turned its attention to the Coromandel Coast on the eastern side of India. Over the ensuing decades, partly through circumstance and partly through political manoeuvring, relatively secure bases were established, most notably in Madras, Bombay and Calcutta, which emerged as the three principal sites of the Raj. Our understanding of this process is, however, fragile. What is clear is that early incursions were secured through negotiations between Company agents and indigenous authorities, the details of which cannot be fully grasped without an intimate knowledge of competing systems of land administration and the laws governing land, as well as an appreciation of regional balances of political power.
The cover of Land, Law and Empire: The Origins of British Territorial Power in India by John Marriott, published by Cambridge University Press in 2025.

Key to this was the relatively small coterie of Company agents who, by forming a branch of subimperialism, effectively conducted affairs in India (see Eric Stokes, The Peasant and the Raj: Studies in Agrarian Society and Peasant Rebellion in Colonial India, Cambridge University Press, 1973). Given that it took six months for a communication from the directors in London to reach India, the agents, legitimately claiming that they knew conditions on the ground best, were able to act autonomously in all spheres of Company endeavour, including the acquisition of land. Under these circumstances, we might have expected some among them to be versed in land law as a precondition for entering into negotiations with indigenous authorities. This, however, was never the case. To the best of my knowledge, no factor was trained in, or indeed possessed even a rudimentary knowledge of, English land law, let alone Mughal or Hindu codes governing the administration of land. The directors were aware of this deficiency and attempted to address it by shipping out small collections of standard legal texts, but it was a futile gesture.

Two urgent questions arise: How did Company agents approach negotiations over land, and to what extent were these conducted within a framework set by English common law? It seems to me that pragmatism, rather than a coherent, unified strategy, held the key to eventual success. In a piece mischievously entitled ‘In Defense of Ignorance’, Lauren Benton surveys recent work on the legal politics of the Atlantic world in the early modern period (Lauren Benton, ‘In Defense of Ignorance: Frameworks for Legal Politics in the Atlantic World’, in Brian Owensby and Richard Ross (eds), Negotiating Legal Intelligibility in British, Iberian and Indigenous America, New York University Press, 2018). In legal negotiations with Native American communities, she argues, there was a clear separation on both sides between intelligibility and understanding. The absence of legal training among colonisers did not compromise their position; indigenous legal codes became intelligible to them as agents came to know them through experience and the application of more familiar legal analogies. Put simply, they developed the skills to read the legal landscape and act strategically, often in a shifting political climate, to reach settlements that furthered their interests. ‘Understanding is overrated,’ Benton concludes, ‘both as a legal capacity and as an object of historical inquiry. Abilities to “read” political-legal constraints and to engage in legal practices with even basic competence, in contrast, brought enormous dividends.’
 
An imagined meeting between Robert Clive and Mir Jafar after the Battle of Palashi in 1757. The Company’s later territorial gains dwarfed the small acquisitions of the preceding century. Painting: Francis Hayman, c. 1760; National Portrait Gallery/Wikimedia Commons.

I see agents acting with the same intelligibility as the Company strove to acquire territory in the seventeenth century. When its interests turned to the Coromandel Coast, the site chosen was an unprepossessing fishing village with few natural advantages. The directors initially disapproved of any notion of establishing a settlement, but the agents recognised the potential of Madras, which, crucially, being located in a region beyond Mughal control, would not be subject to the same intransigence experienced in Surat. Indeed, in what was a febrile political climate punctuated by warring factions, the local nayak, Venkatappa, saw in an alliance with the Company an opportunity to boost trade and strengthen his position against rival kingdoms. The kaul subsequently granted in 1638 contained unprecedented concessions, including the right to build a fort and the authority to govern Madras for two years. Because the nayak did not hold alienable rights over the land, however, the Company viewed the arrangement through the lens of common law as a fief under his suzerainty.

This plot, largely infertile and providing, at best, poor foundations for buildings, measured only four square miles, but it was to become the Company's first permanent settlement in India. The initial kaul was renewed, and little time was lost in building what became Fort St George. The security it offered attracted native artisans seeking refuge from the conflicts. They settled outside the walls in their thousands, and the population soared. By 1680, the population of Madras stood at approximately 300,000. In a remarkable missive to the St George council, Josiah Child, the most rapacious of Company chairmen, declared that the place might well provide the foundation of a permanent English dominion in India.
Fort St George at Madras, depicted in an eighteenth-century print. Founded on the Coromandel Coast in the 1630s, the settlement gave the Company a fortified base beyond Mughal control. Source: detail of a print published by J. Fielding in 1782, in John Marriott’s collection.

The next great centre of empire, Bombay, was acquired and grew under very different circumstances. Since 1534, when Sultan Bahadur signed a treaty conferring rights on the Portuguese, the small island and port had languished through neglect and were generally considered to have few prospects. The beleaguered Company at Surat, however, looked to Bombay as a means of opening up trade along the west coast, but the Portuguese resisted any such move. Then, in one of those remarkable events of historical happenstance, Charles II married the Portuguese Infanta Catharina in 1662. As part of the deal, Alfonso ceded control of Bombay, which became Charles's personal demesne, much to the dismay of the Viceroy of Goa, Antonio de Castro, who declared that the treaty would threaten the Portuguese presence in the region, not least by forcing vital legal issues over ownership onto the agenda. While the terms of the treaty were facilitated by shared legal traditions between the English and Portuguese, the practical realities facing Portuguese landowners who risked losing their estates were much less readily resolved, particularly since many were prepared to organise armed resistance.

Charles regarded Bombay as an expensive liability. Quite apart from the turmoil over landownership, there seemed little prospect of it becoming a major trading centre. He offered to sell the island back to the Portuguese crown, but the asking price was exorbitant. Instead, following lobbying, the Company stepped in to take control. And so it was that in 1668, under the terms of a royal charter, all rights, territories and appurtenances were transferred to the Company in return for an annuity of ten pounds. In language that revealed the extent to which the charter was conceived within English codes of common law dating back to the medieval period, Bombay would remain holden to Charles and his successors ‘as the Manor of East Greenwich, in free and common socage, and not in capite, not by knight’s service’ (John Marriott, Land, Law and Empire: The Origins of British Territorial Power in India, Cambridge University Press, 2025, p. 158). In effect, this form of tenure exempted the Company from traditional obligations associated with landholding, including labour and military service.
Two views of the English fort at Bombay, published by Philip Baldaeus in 1672. The Company took control of Bombay in 1668, amid disputes over land held under Portuguese rule. Source: Philip Baldaeus/Wikimedia Commons.

The Company’s ambitions for Bombay were realised only gradually. Before fortification was completed early in the eighteenth century, the island faced serious problems. The expense of the fort itself, threats from external forces that resulted in its seizure in 1690, land reclamation and even a mutiny that resulted in the capture of the administration for a year all delayed the mission to develop the site as a major trading centre. Against this background emerged a renewed determination to exploit a long-held interest in Bengal. Following a disastrous attempt to capture Chittagong, the chief agent in the region, Job Charnock, sailed up the Ganges in 1690, looking for a suitable permanent site. He chose three small trading villages. At first glance, this pestilential settlement with few trading links was an unlikely option, but situated on the banks of the Ganges, with impenetrable jungle behind it, the site was defensible. Three years later, Charnock died, and so the reputation of this semi-mythical figure as the founder of Calcutta is somewhat misplaced, except that, in retrospect, his initial choice of the site was inspired.

Thus it was that Charles Eyre took over the administration and applied himself to the task of increasing revenue by acquiring land in the immediate vicinity. The three villages soon to become Calcutta were held by a Hindu family as a jaghir, originally granted by Jahangir in recognition of its help in defeating a local maharaja seeking independence. Under Mughal authority, rights to the land, although complicated, would not normally have been transferable to the Company. But events propelled a different course. 
Job Charnock’s tomb and epitaph in Kolkata. Charnock chose the site of the Company’s future Calcutta settlement. Source: Rangan Datta Wiki/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

In 1697, a revolt led by Subha Singh captured Bengal to the west of the Hugli River. The local nawab sought the help of British ships to defeat the rebels, which was agreed to on condition that full tenurial rights over Calcutta be conceded to the Company. These demands were denied; instead, inferior raiyat rights were offered and subsequently accepted, most likely because they included a provision to fortify the new factory. At this point, and with new confidence, Eyre sought to extend his territorial authority. Fully aware that zamindari rights would be resisted by local zamindars, he approached Prince Azim, the Viceroy of Bengal, who acceded to his wishes. Over the ensuing period, Fort William was completed; as in Madras, its protection attracted the settlement of artisans and labourers and attendant increases in revenue, while ever more land came under the control of the Company as zamindar. By 1717, following a concerted campaign of bribery and extortion, the Company received a farman bestowing the right to trade freely in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa and to build a factory on any site of its choosing.

In a process more complicated than I have been able to convey in this short account, the East India Company established during the seventeenth century the necessary but not sufficient conditions for the acquisition of large swathes of India. Given the ignorance among factors of even the rudimentary features of English common law governing land, negotiations were likely pursued through corrupt and coercive means, particularly when advantageous opportunities opened up. The language of common law occasionally appeared in the drafting of agreements, but it was little more than window dressing to convey a spurious authority by lending legal legitimacy to arrangements whose practical foundations lay elsewhere.
 
A coloured engraving of Fort William in Bengal, belonging to the English East India Company. Printed for John Bowles, it is a reissue of the 1754 original by Jan van Ryne. Image: British Library

The Company’s territorial control was confined to small areas around what became the three great presidencies of Madras, Bombay and Calcutta, but the legal, ideological and economic foundations had been laid for the extraordinary land grab of the following centuries. In this respect, land was a vital aspect of Company endeavour. Without land, there was no protection or reliable source of revenue, and ultimately no empire. And yet land also exposed deep fault lines between commerce and conquest, London directors and factors, the Company and rival powers, and between policy and practice. These tensions were not incidental to the Company’s expansion. They were integral to it.

I have been conscious of the multidimensionality of land. If I have tended to focus on the legal and economic dimensions, it is because I lack the detailed knowledge of indigenous traditions of landownership and administration necessary for a detailed investigation of such aspects as identity, belonging and memory. I await with interest to see whether others better versed in indigenous land cultures rise to this challenge.

Professor John Marriott is a visiting fellow at Kellogg College, University of Oxford, and the author of Land, Law and Empire: The Origins of British Territorial Power in India (Cambridge University Press, 2025).

item.title: The Daily Star – China celebrates its scientists. Why doesn't Bangladesh?
item.description:
In August 2026, shopping malls in Heze and Zibo, two cities in Shandong province, voluntarily cleared their most prized advertising screens. In place of film stars and product launches, they displayed giant portraits of scientists. The idea spread. Commuters in Zhengzhou began walking past the faces of rocket scientist Qian Xuesen and nuclear physicist Deng Jiaxian on their way to work, and similar displays appeared in Hangzhou, Hefei and several other provinces.

The faces chosen tell their own stories. Qian Xuesen, the father of China's missile and space programme. Tu Youyou, who discovered the malaria drug artemisinin and became China's first Nobel laureate in medicine. Yuan Longping, the father of hybrid rice, whose seeds helped feed hundreds of millions of people. Some of the posters call them society's real "top stars".

The billboards did not make China a scientific power. China already spends 2.69 per cent of its very large economy on research; the posters are the visible tip of decades of investment in laboratories, universities and research budgets. But public recognition and research feed each other. A billboard cannot build a laboratory. It can tell a generation why laboratories matter, and a laboratory without public respect will not attract young people for long.
Posters featuring Chinese scientists Qian Xuesen and Deng Jiaxian at the Convention and Exhibition Centre metro station in Zhengzhou, Henan province, China, on 27 August 2026. China spends 2.69 per cent of its GDP on research, with public recognition accompanying decades of investment in laboratories, universities and scientific development. Photo: VCG

Now look at our billboards. Who appears on them, apart from models? When one of us does something remarkable, we gather to pull them down. When someone tries to work for the country outside party politics, we tear their reputation apart before the work has even begun.

The figures bear out this feeling.

The arithmetic of neglect

Bangladesh spends 0.30 per cent of its GDP on research and development. The figure comes from the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics' first R&D survey, published in 2024 with data for the 2020–21 fiscal year. The share has been falling: 0.35 per cent in 2018–19 and 0.31 per cent the following year. In monetary terms, the country spent Tk 10,481 crore, or about Tk 620 per person per year. That was roughly seven dollars at the exchange rate of the time, and about five at today's rate. It is less than two taka a day, less than the price of a cup of roadside tea.

South Korea spent 5.13 per cent of its GDP on R&D in 2024, second in the world only to Israel, which spends more than twenty times our share.

This is no longer an outsider's complaint. At a research grants ceremony in Dhaka on 24 August, Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury called our 0.3 per cent one of the lowest rates among peer middle-income countries. Citing BBS data, he added that manufacturing firms spend, on average, less than Tk 500 per worker annually on research and innovation.

item.title: The Daily Star – What the Rohingya genocide verdict means for Gaza
item.description:
On Thursday, hundreds of Rohingya sat in rows of red plastic chairs in a Cox's Bazar camp hall and watched the International Court of Justice read out its verdict, which took almost three hours.

By nine votes to six, the judges found that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya in 2017.

It was the first time the court had held a state, rather than individuals, responsible for the crime itself. For those in the camps, that was recognition, and it was a long time coming.

However, for lawyers and diplomats elsewhere, it also raised another question: what does it mean for South Africa's case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza?

The temptation to read the verdict as a victory for either side should be resisted. The verdict does not convict Israel, nor does it lower the legal threshold for proving genocide.

What it does is knock out several of the shelters that states fighting armed groups have used to argue that genocide cannot be the charge. It also shifts the fight from definitions to evidence.

To begin with, the ruling binds only Myanmar and The Gambia, and it concerns a different conflict with a different body of evidence.

Alan Baker, a former legal adviser to Israel's foreign ministry, told Jewish Insider that nobody should exaggerate its implications. On that much, he is right.
Rohingya refugees gather at a camp in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, on 19 November 2026 to watch the International Court of Justice deliver its judgment in The Gambia's genocide case against Myanmar. The court found Myanmar responsible for committing genocide against the Rohingya in 2017. Photo: Reuters

Time is on his side too. Israel filed its defence in March this year, and South Africa's next pleading is due on 22 November next year, with Israel's reply due on 22 May 2029.

So, it would be unwise to expect a judgment before 2030 or 2031, by which time the bench may very well look different.

In other words, whatever the judges said last week, the question of Israel's responsibility for genocide in Gaza remains very much open.

The difficulty of establishing a state's responsibility for genocide becomes clearer when we look at the cases the court has decided against such claims.

In 2007, in the case Bosnia brought against Serbia, the court ruled that the massacre at Srebrenica in July 1995 constituted genocide. But it did not hold Serbia responsible for committing it or helping to carry it out.

Instead, it found that Serbia had failed to prevent the genocide and punish those responsible, including by failing to cooperate fully with the Yugoslav tribunal in the pursuit of Ratko Mladić.

Bosnia had sought compensation but received no such relief. The court said there was no proof that the massacre would have been prevented had Serbia acted as it should have. It also made clear that the rest of the war in Bosnia did not amount to genocide.

Things went no better for Croatia in its case against Serbia. In 2015, the court rejected Croatia's genocide claim over alleged crimes against Croats during the 1991–95 war by 15 votes to two.
Palestinians walk near the rubble of buildings destroyed during the war in Gaza City on 28 October 2026. The ICJ's ruling on the Rohingya genocide has raised questions about its implications for South Africa's case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza. Photo: Reuters

It also unanimously rejected Serbia's counterclaim over alleged genocide against ethnic Serbs during and after Operation Storm in August 1995.

For years, these two rulings were cited as evidence of just how difficult it was to hold a state responsible for genocide.

Critics argued that the court had set an exceptionally high bar, particularly when it came to establishing genocidal intent from a state's actions. The Myanmar case is the first time a state has crossed that threshold.

This time around, the court has not abandoned that test. To establish genocidal intent from a state's conduct, it must still be the only reasonable inference from the evidence.

What the judges clarified, in paragraph 443, is that genocidal intent can exist alongside other intentions, as long as they do not contradict each other.

Myanmar offered three explanations: it was fighting an armed group, it wanted to push the Rohingya out rather than wipe them out, and it was punishing alleged insurgents. The court rejected all three.

Anyone following the Gaza case will recognise some of the same arguments: Israel says it is fighting terrorism, while its military operations have repeatedly displaced civilians. Critics also point to what they see as a desire for revenge after 7 October.

But the Myanmar ruling makes one thing clear: a state cannot escape a genocide allegation simply by arguing that it was pursuing military objectives.
Rohingya refugees fleeing Myanmar's military crackdown walk along an embankment in Palang Khali, near Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, on 2 November 2017. The ICJ found that at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed and around 326,000 had their homes burned during the 2017 campaign. Photo: Reuters

Since genocide can take place during an armed conflict, the existence of a military campaign does not, in itself, rule out genocidal intent.

The numbers also challenge what people assume genocide looks like. The court found that at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed, at least 1,834 rapes were committed and around 326,000 people had their homes burned.

Ten thousand deaths represent about 1.2 per cent of the 815,000 Rohingya in northern Rakhine, yet the court still found genocide. Destroying a group, the judges said, does not mean killing all or even most of its members.

One of Israel's favourite defences also took a hit: that a state intent on destroying a people would not bother to limit civilian deaths.

Myanmar said the same, but the court replied that failing to take every opportunity to destroy a group does not rule out genocidal intent. Warnings, safe zones and pauses in fighting count as evidence, but they cannot settle the matter alone.

Then there is the question of proof. In the Bosnia and Croatia cases, the judges relied heavily on the Yugoslav war crimes tribunal. Myanmar had no such body, so the court turned to UN investigators.

It judged their methods rigorous without adopting their legal conclusions, and said Myanmar's refusal to cooperate gave it greater freedom to draw conclusions.

That could matter for Israel. A UN inquiry chaired by Navi Pillay concluded in September last year that Israel had committed genocide, a finding Israel rejects.
Judges at the International Court of Justice in The Hague, Netherlands, deliver a ruling on provisional measures in South Africa's genocide case against Israel on 26 January 2024. Although the Myanmar judgment does not bind Israel, its reasoning on genocidal intent and military objectives could influence the court's consideration of the Gaza case. Photo: Reuters

Israel's side has a fair point that UN reports do not automatically meet a court's standard of proof. The ruling shows that the judges will use such reports, not accept them wholesale.

Some of the sharpest warnings have come from Israel's supporters. A think tank funded by pro-Israeli groups argues that, although the court has retained the existing legal test, its interpretation could make it easier to infer genocidal intent from a state's conduct.

It warns that the reasoning could have consequences for Western militaries fighting armed groups.

Meanwhile, in paragraph 487, the court made a significant change to its interpretation of the duty to prevent genocide. In the Bosnia case, it had held that a state could be found to have breached that duty only if genocide actually occurred.

The court has now clarified a point left unresolved in the Bosnia case, ruling that a state's responsibility for breaching its preventive obligation does not depend on genocide actually having occurred.

The obligation arises when a state knows, or should normally have known, of such a risk, and requires it to use all reasonably available means to prevent it.

That has implications well beyond Israel. Germany, which has supplied military equipment to Israel, is already facing a separate case brought by Nicaragua at the ICJ over its support for Israel and alleged failure to prevent genocide in Gaza.

The new interpretation could make it harder for Germany, and potentially other states providing military assistance, to argue that their preventive obligations depend on genocide first being established.
Rows of gravestones at the Srebrenica–Potočari Memorial and Cemetery in Bosnia and Herzegovina honour victims of the July 1995 massacre. In its 2007 judgment, the ICJ recognised the massacre as genocide but did not hold Serbia responsible for committing it, illustrating the difficulty of establishing a state's responsibility for genocide. Photo: Wikipedia

Their conduct, knowledge of the risk and capacity to influence Israel's actions could become central to determining whether they have fulfilled those obligations.

Israel's defenders say the situations are not comparable, and they have evidence to support their argument.

They argue that the evidence in Myanmar, including decades of anti-Rohingya hate speech, the systematic destruction of villages, mass rape and attacks on children, has no direct equivalent in Gaza, or at least has not been established there in the same way.

They also point to one particular element of the court's finding: measures intended to prevent births. Israel's defenders say there is nothing comparable in Gaza.

South Africa replies that military operations have created conditions that affect births, which Israel denies.

The dissent also deserves attention. Six judges disagreed with the finding of genocide, though they did not dispute the scale of the atrocities committed against the Rohingya.

Their central objection was that the evidence did not sufficiently establish Myanmar's specific intention to physically or biologically destroy the group, rather than forcibly remove it.

They warned against treating mass displacement, persecution and the destruction of a community's social foundations as sufficient proof of genocide, arguing that this risked blurring the distinction between genocide and ethnic cleansing.
Palestinians gather near a house targeted by an Israeli airstrike following a warning from the Israeli military for residents to evacuate, in Gaza City on 30 October 2026. The ICJ's Myanmar ruling makes clear that the pursuit of military objectives does not, in itself, rule out genocidal intent. Photo: Reuters

The majority, however, considered the killings, serious bodily and mental harm, and measures intended to prevent births, together with the wider pattern of conduct. It concluded that the evidence established genocidal intent beyond reasonable doubt.

The disagreement, therefore, was not over whether the Rohingya had suffered atrocities, but over what those atrocities proved about Myanmar's intentions.

Politics, however, may matter more than any of this. Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands and the UK jointly presented an argument in the Myanmar case that the majority later embraced.

It is far from certain that they will stand behind a similar finding on Gaza, and Germany, shaped by its responsibility for the Holocaust, looks the least likely.

Pillay has become a target too: Washington accused her of trying to lower the bar for genocide. Her defenders call that baseless, noting that no single judge decides a verdict.

Even a favourable ruling would need politics to carry it. The court's rulings are binding, but beyond referring non-compliance to the UN Security Council, it has no means of enforcing them.

On Thursday, hundreds of Rohingya sat in rows of red plastic chairs in a Cox's Bazar camp hall and watched the International Court of Justice read out its verdict, which took almost three hours.

By nine votes to six, the judges found that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya in 2017.

It was the first time the court had held a state, rather than individuals, responsible for the crime itself. For those in the camps, that was recognition, and it was a long time coming.

However, for lawyers and diplomats elsewhere, it also raised another question: what does it mean for South Africa's case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza?

The temptation to read the verdict as a victory for either side should be resisted. The verdict does not convict Israel, nor does it lower the legal threshold for proving genocide.

What it does is knock out several of the shelters that states fighting armed groups have used to argue that genocide cannot be the charge. It also shifts the fight from definitions to evidence.

To begin with, the ruling binds only Myanmar and The Gambia, and it concerns a different conflict with a different body of evidence.

Alan Baker, a former legal adviser to Israel's foreign ministry, told Jewish Insider that nobody should exaggerate its implications. On that much, he is right.
Rohingya refugees gather at a camp in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, on 19 November 2026 to watch the International Court of Justice deliver its judgment in The Gambia's genocide case against Myanmar. The court found Myanmar responsible for committing genocide against the Rohingya in 2017. Photo: Reuters

Time is on his side too. Israel filed its defence in March this year, and South Africa's next pleading is due on 22 November next year, with Israel's reply due on 22 May 2029.

So, it would be unwise to expect a judgment before 2030 or 2031, by which time the bench may very well look different.

In other words, whatever the judges said last week, the question of Israel's responsibility for genocide in Gaza remains very much open.

The difficulty of establishing a state's responsibility for genocide becomes clearer when we look at the cases the court has decided against such claims.

In 2007, in the case Bosnia brought against Serbia, the court ruled that the massacre at Srebrenica in July 1995 constituted genocide. But it did not hold Serbia responsible for committing it or helping to carry it out.

Instead, it found that Serbia had failed to prevent the genocide and punish those responsible, including by failing to cooperate fully with the Yugoslav tribunal in the pursuit of Ratko Mladić.

Bosnia had sought compensation but received no such relief. The court said there was no proof that the massacre would have been prevented had Serbia acted as it should have. It also made clear that the rest of the war in Bosnia did not amount to genocide.

Things went no better for Croatia in its case against Serbia. In 2015, the court rejected Croatia's genocide claim over alleged crimes against Croats during the 1991–95 war by 15 votes to two.
Palestinians walk near the rubble of buildings destroyed during the war in Gaza City on 28 October 2026. The ICJ's ruling on the Rohingya genocide has raised questions about its implications for South Africa's case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza. Photo: Reuters

It also unanimously rejected Serbia's counterclaim over alleged genocide against ethnic Serbs during and after Operation Storm in August 1995.

For years, these two rulings were cited as evidence of just how difficult it was to hold a state responsible for genocide.

Critics argued that the court had set an exceptionally high bar, particularly when it came to establishing genocidal intent from a state's actions. The Myanmar case is the first time a state has crossed that threshold.

This time around, the court has not abandoned that test. To establish genocidal intent from a state's conduct, it must still be the only reasonable inference from the evidence.

What the judges clarified, in paragraph 443, is that genocidal intent can exist alongside other intentions, as long as they do not contradict each other.

Myanmar offered three explanations: it was fighting an armed group, it wanted to push the Rohingya out rather than wipe them out, and it was punishing alleged insurgents. The court rejected all three.

Anyone following the Gaza case will recognise some of the same arguments: Israel says it is fighting terrorism, while its military operations have repeatedly displaced civilians. Critics also point to what they see as a desire for revenge after 7 October.

But the Myanmar ruling makes one thing clear: a state cannot escape a genocide allegation simply by arguing that it was pursuing military objectives.
Rohingya refugees fleeing Myanmar's military crackdown walk along an embankment in Palang Khali, near Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, on 2 November 2017. The ICJ found that at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed and around 326,000 had their homes burned during the 2017 campaign. Photo: Reuters

Since genocide can take place during an armed conflict, the existence of a military campaign does not, in itself, rule out genocidal intent.

The numbers also challenge what people assume genocide looks like. The court found that at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed, at least 1,834 rapes were committed and around 326,000 people had their homes burned.

Ten thousand deaths represent about 1.2 per cent of the 815,000 Rohingya in northern Rakhine, yet the court still found genocide. Destroying a group, the judges said, does not mean killing all or even most of its members.

One of Israel's favourite defences also took a hit: that a state intent on destroying a people would not bother to limit civilian deaths.

Myanmar said the same, but the court replied that failing to take every opportunity to destroy a group does not rule out genocidal intent. Warnings, safe zones and pauses in fighting count as evidence, but they cannot settle the matter alone.

Then there is the question of proof. In the Bosnia and Croatia cases, the judges relied heavily on the Yugoslav war crimes tribunal. Myanmar had no such body, so the court turned to UN investigators.

It judged their methods rigorous without adopting their legal conclusions, and said Myanmar's refusal to cooperate gave it greater freedom to draw conclusions.

That could matter for Israel. A UN inquiry chaired by Navi Pillay concluded in September last year that Israel had committed genocide, a finding Israel rejects.
Judges at the International Court of Justice in The Hague, Netherlands, deliver a ruling on provisional measures in South Africa's genocide case against Israel on 26 January 2024. Although the Myanmar judgment does not bind Israel, its reasoning on genocidal intent and military objectives could influence the court's consideration of the Gaza case. Photo: Reuters

Israel's side has a fair point that UN reports do not automatically meet a court's standard of proof. The ruling shows that the judges will use such reports, not accept them wholesale.

Some of the sharpest warnings have come from Israel's supporters. A think tank funded by pro-Israeli groups argues that, although the court has retained the existing legal test, its interpretation could make it easier to infer genocidal intent from a state's conduct.

It warns that the reasoning could have consequences for Western militaries fighting armed groups.

Meanwhile, in paragraph 487, the court made a significant change to its interpretation of the duty to prevent genocide. In the Bosnia case, it had held that a state could be found to have breached that duty only if genocide actually occurred.

The court has now clarified a point left unresolved in the Bosnia case, ruling that a state's responsibility for breaching its preventive obligation does not depend on genocide actually having occurred.

The obligation arises when a state knows, or should normally have known, of such a risk, and requires it to use all reasonably available means to prevent it.

That has implications well beyond Israel. Germany, which has supplied military equipment to Israel, is already facing a separate case brought by Nicaragua at the ICJ over its support for Israel and alleged failure to prevent genocide in Gaza.

The new interpretation could make it harder for Germany, and potentially other states providing military assistance, to argue that their preventive obligations depend on genocide first being established.
Rows of gravestones at the Srebrenica–Potočari Memorial and Cemetery in Bosnia and Herzegovina honour victims of the July 1995 massacre. In its 2007 judgment, the ICJ recognised the massacre as genocide but did not hold Serbia responsible for committing it, illustrating the difficulty of establishing a state's responsibility for genocide. Photo: Wikipedia

Their conduct, knowledge of the risk and capacity to influence Israel's actions could become central to determining whether they have fulfilled those obligations.

Israel's defenders say the situations are not comparable, and they have evidence to support their argument.

They argue that the evidence in Myanmar, including decades of anti-Rohingya hate speech, the systematic destruction of villages, mass rape and attacks on children, has no direct equivalent in Gaza, or at least has not been established there in the same way.

They also point to one particular element of the court's finding: measures intended to prevent births. Israel's defenders say there is nothing comparable in Gaza.

South Africa replies that military operations have created conditions that affect births, which Israel denies.

The dissent also deserves attention. Six judges disagreed with the finding of genocide, though they did not dispute the scale of the atrocities committed against the Rohingya.

Their central objection was that the evidence did not sufficiently establish Myanmar's specific intention to physically or biologically destroy the group, rather than forcibly remove it.

They warned against treating mass displacement, persecution and the destruction of a community's social foundations as sufficient proof of genocide, arguing that this risked blurring the distinction between genocide and ethnic cleansing.
Palestinians gather near a house targeted by an Israeli airstrike following a warning from the Israeli military for residents to evacuate, in Gaza City on 30 October 2026. The ICJ's Myanmar ruling makes clear that the pursuit of military objectives does not, in itself, rule out genocidal intent. Photo: Reuters

The majority, however, considered the killings, serious bodily and mental harm, and measures intended to prevent births, together with the wider pattern of conduct. It concluded that the evidence established genocidal intent beyond reasonable doubt.

The disagreement, therefore, was not over whether the Rohingya had suffered atrocities, but over what those atrocities proved about Myanmar's intentions.

Politics, however, may matter more than any of this. Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands and the UK jointly presented an argument in the Myanmar case that the majority later embraced.

It is far from certain that they will stand behind a similar finding on Gaza, and Germany, shaped by its responsibility for the Holocaust, looks the least likely.

Britain has called for an urgent Council session on Myanmar, yet Washington, which holds a veto there, has yet to take a position on the ruling.

If the court ever rules against Israel, the same Council would decide what that finding is worth.

item.title: The Daily Star – From decoration to storytelling: The evolution of children's book illustration in Bangladesh
item.description:
For decades in Bangladesh, the image inside a children’s book was viewed primarily as alankaran, a decorative ornament placed on the page to break up dense blocks of text or visually mirror what the author had already written. If a story described a young boy standing beside a banyan tree, the artist was expected simply to draw a boy beside a banyan tree. The writer’s name dominated the cover in bold lettering, while the artist remained an anonymous craftsman, rarely credited on the cover.

Today, a profound paradigm shift is underway. Children’s book illustration in Bangladesh has broken free from its subordinate status, evolving into an autonomous art form rooted in sequential storytelling, visual metaphor and equal creative partnership. To trace this remarkable evolution is to understand how Bangladesh’s cultural landscape, printing technology, NGO interventions and dedicated visionaries transformed a commercial afterthought into a confident, respected artistic discipline.

The foundational canvas (1970s–1980s)

In the immediate wake of the 1971 Liberation War, Bangladeshi children’s literature drew its visual identity from the nation's premier fine artists. The foundational canvas was established by iconic figures who brought artistic dignity to print media. Among them, Qayyum Chowdhury stands as an iconic figure in Bangladeshi illustration history, working alongside contemporaries and artists such as Rafiqun Nabi, Hashem Khan, Shishir Bhattacharjee, Afzal Hossain, Farida Zaman, Abul Barq Alvi and Samarjit Roy Chowdhury. The artwork and cartoons of these early decades provided the visual backdrop for generations growing up in the 1980s.
The cover of Kedo by Ekhlasuddin Ahmed, illustrated by Qayyum Chowdhury, features a wide-eyed cat beneath a patterned blue shape. Drawing inspiration from indigenous folk heritage, Chowdhury fused traditional motifs with modernist graphic clarity, championing the idea that a book's visual identity should convey its literary essence before the first line is read.

These foundational figures did not merely illustrate stories; they established the delta's visual grammar, diversifying their artistic practices across textbooks, juvenile magazines, book jackets and political cartoons to construct a sovereign cultural aesthetic.

Qayyum Chowdhury (1932–2014) revolutionised the relationship between literature and graphic design. Drawing inspiration from indigenous folk heritage, alpana floor patterns, nakshi kantha embroidery, and deltaic flora and fauna, he fused traditional motifs with modernist graphic clarity. Over half a century, Chowdhury illustrated children's verse and folklore and designed thousands of iconic book covers, championing the idea that a book’s visual identity should convey its literary essence before the first line is read.

Hashem Khan (b. 1941) became the quintessential architect of children’s visual imagination in post-liberation Bangladesh. Commissioned shortly after 1971 to illustrate primary school textbooks for the National Curriculum and Textbook Board (NCTB), Hashem Khan introduced millions of students to the foundational aesthetics of their sovereign nation through vibrant primary palettes: deltaic greens, river blues and sunlit yellows. Through his tender, empathetic visual depictions of the Liberation War in juvenile fiction and his institutional work with the Bangladesh Shishu Academy and Kochi-Kachar Mela, he established early visual literacy as a cornerstone of childhood development.

Rafiqun Nabi (b. 1943), celebrated affectionately as Ronobi, brought social dynamism and raw kinetic life to children’s and adolescent literature. While widely renowned for his satirical street-child creation Tokai, Ronobi’s work across children's monthlies such as Kishore Bangla showcased an expressive mastery of woodcut prints and spontaneous pen-and-ink drawings. His portrayals of village youths, street life and folklore treated young minds with dignity, blending humour, realism and emotional gravity.

Alongside these masters, prolific illustrators such as Pranesh Kumar Mandal and Kalam Mahmood dominated the popular reading boom of the 1980s. Working under rigorous press deadlines, their dynamic, high-contrast ink illustrations defined the covers and interiors of popular juvenile paperbacks, ghost stories and mystery thrillers (including Sheba Prokashoni’s widely circulated series), cementing an enduring visual bond with young readers.

During these early decades, illustration was closely tied to newspapers, literary periodicals and state-sponsored publications such as Shishu magazine. However, artists faced severe structural and technical constraints. Mahbubul Haque, publisher and founder of Ikrimikri and a veteran designer, recalls the rigid parameters under which artists worked in traditional newsrooms and commercial presses: "Back when I worked in newspaper illustration, artists were simply assigned a fixed column space, say, a specific number of inches, and told what to draw. I constantly questioned why we couldn't approach the story from different visual angles. Eventually, I insisted on reading full story scripts first, which allowed us to create far more focused, imaginative, and impactful imagery."
The cover of Halum! Alum! (2016), featuring a tiger and its cubs, illustrated by Biplob Chakraborty.

Furthermore, commercial publishers during the 1970s and 1980s operated under strict paper metrics, adhering rigidly to 16-page printing units (formas). This practice frequently disrupted narrative flow and resulted in awkward page layouts. Children's literature was also conceptually conflated with adolescent fiction; true picture books tailored specifically for toddlers and early childhood visual development were virtually non-existent.

The 1990s turning point: NGO influx, DTP technology and early reading

The 1990s marked a dramatic turning point in Bangladeshi children's publishing, driven by two major catalysts: international non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and the digital revolution in pre-press production. As Sabbyasachi Mistry notes, corporate expansion and a massive influx of investment into the development sector reshaped the industry: "The 1990s marked a pivotal shift in the industry as corporate expansion and a massive surge in the NGO sector created high demand for illustrations, educational materials, and animation. This influx transformed illustration from a niche creative pursuit into a viable professional career path. Illustrators created message-driven artwork, clip art, educational booklets, advertising graphics, and mainstream children’s literature."

Prominent illustrators, including Yusuf Ali Notun, Sujon Chowdhury, Yaqub and Raju, left an indelible imprint on national board textbooks such as Amar Bangla Boi, establishing recognisable characters for millions of schoolchildren under the National Curriculum and Textbook Board (NCTB). Simultaneously, organisations such as UNICEF introduced age-graded reading materials, early childhood healthcare graphics and international publishing standards. This reshaped how publishers viewed target demographics, distinguishing early childhood literature from adolescent fiction.
An illustrated two-page spread from a Bengali children's story shows a man speaking to villagers and a larger scene depicting an encounter between two characters. Illustrations help young readers follow events, anticipate what happens next and understand feelings and moods that words alone might not convey.

This operational transformation coincided with the rapid shift from manual artwork to digital pre-press workflows. Mahbubul Haque vividly recalls the almost sacred atmosphere of early desktop publishing (DTP) houses in Dhaka during the mid-1990s: "That period marked the arrival of graphic design and digital tools. I remember going to specialised Desktop Publishing (DTP) houses to learn Photoshop and scan line art. Computer rooms had strict protocols; we even had to take off our shoes before entering, and handling film tabs was tightly controlled. Compared to modern workflows, scanning and layout processes back then were far more complex and time-consuming."

Late 1990s and 2000s

Towards the end of the century, as the market expanded, Bangladeshi illustrators sought to develop a distinct visual identity that reflected local cultural heritage while responding to commercial demands. Illustrators turned away from generic Western models to embrace traditional South Asian aesthetic traditions. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, illustrators increasingly adopted line drawings inspired by Oriental art styles, characterised by dynamic thick-and-thin strokes. To achieve visual localisation for young Bangladeshi audiences, artists drew inspiration from traditional artistic heritage, including Mughal and Rajput miniatures and local Gazi's pot paintings (Gazi-r Pot).
The cover of Gacher Kotha Fuler Kotha(2024) by Dwijen Sharma, featuring a colourful botanical illustration attributed to Biren Som.

However, this artistic renaissance encountered commercial realities. Strict NGO production deadlines and tight publisher turnarounds forced many artists to simplify their techniques into flatter line drawings for faster output. Simultaneously, mainstream commercial publishing was dominated by cost-cutting practices. Most commercial houses focused on flooding the market with cheaply produced books, minimising expenditure on ink, paper quality and artist honoraria.

Refusing to accept this compromise, a handful of creative visionaries broke away from commercial norms to advocate for holistic book design and professional dignity for illustrators. Mahbubul Haque points out: "When we examined the commercial publishing landscape, we found that most publishers focused strictly on minimising costs to dump cheap books into the market. We broke away from that approach to produce quality illustrations ourselves."

A publisher must plan a book holistically. That plan includes determining appropriate content for contemporary society and choosing an illustrator whose artistic style and character design fit the story. Haque also initiated a philosophy of equal co-crediting: "Storytelling is not confined to text alone; text and illustration together create a complete narrative. Therefore, we give equal weight and prominent credit to both the author and the illustrator. If an illustrator wishes to introduce a creative twist to convey the story better visually, we consult with the author to accommodate it, ensuring the book best serves young readers."
The cover of Amer Bol Jamer Bol by Shamsul Haque, featuring colourful illustrations of children and dragonflies by Syed Enayet Hossain.

Rise of picture books and visual storytellers

Over the last decade, walking into the children’s section of a bookshop in Bangladesh has become a noticeably different experience. Where shelves were once lined with text-heavy paperbacks carrying only the occasional black-and-white sketch, there is now an explosion of vibrant, thoughtfully designed picture books. Led by specialised publishers such as Mayurpankhi, Ikrimikri and Little Ummah, the country’s children’s literature is undergoing a quiet, colourful reinvention.

Much of this change comes down to how we understand a child's first encounter with a book. For a long time, books were treated primarily as tools for reading lessons, with pictures thrown in simply to make the pages look pretty. Research shows that a child’s relationship with storytelling begins long before they learn the alphabet. Years before they can decode a single sentence, toddlers are already "reading" the world around them, studying facial expressions, making sense of colours and following visual cues.

Mitia Osman, the publisher and founder of Mayurpankhi, points out that this shift in mindset went hand in hand with a leap in printing technology: “Printing technology has significantly improved over time. Earlier artists drew beautifully; illustrations by Sukumar Ray or Satyajit Ray that we grew up with were stunning, but the printing technology back then was letterpress. Even though it gave us pioneering works in children's literature illustration, they couldn't render them with full fidelity. What we started doing was creating true picture books, which was rare before. Previously, books were heavily text-based. Children don't just read words; their relationship with books starts from birth. Before they can read text, they look at pictures.”
The cover of Pakhider Pathshala (2023), a colourful children's book featuring two young characters surrounded by birds and foliage. Specialised publishers such as Mayurpankhi have contributed to the expansion of thoughtfully designed picture books, moving children's literature beyond text-heavy publications with occasional illustrations.

This early visual connection is where lifelong reading habits are truly born. A great picture book does not just tell a story; it gently teaches a child how stories work. By following the illustrations across a page, young readers discover cause and effect, learn to anticipate what happens next and pick up on feelings and moods that words alone might not convey. When a child hears an unfamiliar word, a vivid picture gives them an immediate visual clue, helping them grasp new ideas naturally without feeling tested.

More than anything, illustrations remove the fear of reading. A wall of uninterrupted text can feel intimidating to a young learner, turning reading into a chore. Picture books, by contrast, make the experience playful and interactive. They invite parents and children to sit together, point at the pages and talk about what they see. That shared warmth turns reading into a comforting ritual rather than schoolwork, sparking an affection for books that stays with children as they grow.

As awareness of early learning has grown, Bangladeshi parents have become far more eager to introduce books at an early age. As Mitia Osman observes, “That's why we produce specialised visual books so children build early visual literacy and develop a lifelong love of reading. With social media and modern parenting awareness, parents also understand the necessity of early visual learning.”
The cover of Chhotoder Hashir Golpo by Sadeka Shafiullah, illustrated by Hashem Khan, depicts two children surrounded by birds against a colourful background.

Alongside better printing and early reading habits, there is also a conscious effort to bring storytelling back home. For decades, illustrated literature in Bangladesh was dominated by translated foreign tales. Generations grew up on inexpensive, beautifully illustrated Soviet translations of Russian fairy tales from Raduga Publishers or familiar collections of the Arabian Nights. While those stories sparked incredible wonder, they also meant that Bangladeshi children spent their formative reading years wandering through foreign snowscapes and distant desert kingdoms, with very few illustrated books reflecting the world outside their own windows.

Today’s publishers are working to change that, ensuring that local culture and everyday surroundings are celebrated with the same visual care. As Osman explains, building that local library takes deliberate effort: “We have educational storybooks focusing on local themes like the Sundarbans or Bangladesh's national flower and fruit. However, classics and folk tales form a huge part of children's literature globally. When I entered publishing, original local stories for children were very scarce in the market compared to reprints of classics.”

By introducing children to the mangrove forests of the Sundarbans, the seasonal rhythms of the delta and relatable neighbourhood adventures, modern picture books are doing something vital. They are showing young readers that their own culture is rich with magic and meaning, proving that the simple joy of turning a page can help a child fall in love not only with reading but also with the world they call home. This technological and structural evolution paved the way for a new generation of visual storytellers, including Mehedi Haque Tonmoy, Mahtab Rashid, Nabidur Rahman Munna, Shamim Hossain and Shamim Ahmed.
The cover of Megh Rajkonna by Kakoli Pradhan, illustrated by Shamim Ahmed, depicts a princess riding a giant bird through a colourful sky filled with clouds and fantastical characters.

For children's book illustrator Shamim Ahmed, whose 12-year career reflects the wider transformation of the industry, entering illustration meant challenging old paradigms:

"When I first started working seriously with illustration, around twelve years ago, the area of children’s books in Bangladesh was quite different from what we see today. A typical children's book was still largely text-based. The story was written first, and illustrations were often added afterwards to support or decorate the text... The general understanding of illustration was closer to something that made the page attractive or visually represented what the writer had already described."

Acknowledging early mentors and contemporaries, Shamim Ahmed describes his turning point between 2014 and 2016. Influenced by international visual narrative masters such as Oliver Jeffers and his seminal work The Heart and the Bottle, and drawing on his background in architecture to structure spatial composition and visual rhythm, Ahmed redefined the relationship between text and image: "I don't see the illustrator as someone who merely visualises the writer's sentences. Ideally, the writer and illustrator are two storytellers working with different languages as a team. One works primarily through words; the other works through drawings, composition, rhythm, gesture, colour, silence and visual metaphor. Sometimes an illustration can even contradict the apparent text and reveal something hidden between the words."

Human touch in the age of sequential storytelling

As Bangladeshi children’s book illustration moves forward, it faces both exciting opportunities and nuanced challenges. One major professional hurdle remains mastering sequential narrative consistency across an entire publication. As Mitia Osman explains, "The new generation of artists is exposed to global picture book trends via social media. However, in Bangladesh, finding illustrators who can execute sequential storytelling throughout an entire book remains very difficult. Creating a single beautiful drawing is quite different from maintaining visual consistency across a story narrative."

Yet the future remains bright. Younger artists seamlessly blend traditional media, including pencil, ink, watercolour, batik, paper craft and collage, with digital pre-press tools, bringing local folklore, urban landscapes and contemporary themes to life for young minds.

In an era increasingly dominated by automated, AI-generated images, Bangladeshi visual storytellers reaffirm the value of human craft and emotional resonance. As Shamim Ahmed reflects on his journey: "In the world of AI, the images created by human hand will hold the mark of truth in the coming days. An image does not always need to explain everything to children. It can leave something unresolved, invite them to imagine or allow them to discover a story beyond the words of their own. 'What can an image say that the words cannot?' That feels very much like my 12-year journey in one sentence."

Through five decades of artistic evolution, Bangladeshi children's book illustration has transformed from a mere background decoration into a powerful, living language, one that continues to inspire, spark imagination and nurture the young minds of tomorrow.

Adrin Sarwar is a sub-editor at Slow Reads.
